title: 10,500-year-old timbers rise from lakebed
dek: Wood and stone emerge from a German lake, offering rare insight into Mesolithic life.
body: About 20 metres beneath Lake Arendsee in Saxony-Anhalt, underwater archaeologists have recovered worked timbers, stone tools and animal bones. The finds were made during spring 2026 investigations by the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology of Saxony-Anhalt. Large and small pieces of worked wood, including a 1.6-metre post, suggest human activity at the ancient lakeshore.

The most striking find is a wooden post that preserves clear evidence of felling and working. Split planks up to 1.3 metres long were also recovered. Researchers suspect the timbers may have belonged to a constructed feature, potentially even a hut. However, no building plan or other evidence has yet established that the wood formed part of a dwelling. Describing the site as a permanent settlement remains premature.

Around 10,500 years ago, Central European communities relied on hunting, fishing and gathering. Even if a structure is eventually identified at Arendsee, this would not necessarily indicate permanent occupation. Hunter-gatherers could construct substantial features at camps that were occupied temporarily or revisited seasonally. The discovery matters because of the exceptional survival of worked wood from the Mesolithic period.

Evidence for structures from this period is often preserved only indirectly, through postholes or changes in soil colour. The waterlogged environment at Arendsee has preserved the timber itself, including traces of prehistoric woodworking. A salt dome beneath the lake has caused sections of the lakebed to submerge former shorelines. Sediment subsequently covered remains along these ancient shores, creating conditions capable of preserving organic material.

The lake has previously produced discoveries from several periods, including Neolithic fish weirs and medieval watercraft. Researchers are now using underwater technology to investigate the prehistoric landscape in greater detail. A remotely operated underwater vehicle, deployed with the Fraunhofer Institute in Ilmenau, has produced high-resolution sonar imagery of the former shoreline. The survey is helping archaeologists identify areas for future investigation and plan more targeted dives.

Researchers hope to conduct dendrochronological analysis using surviving tree rings, though dating ancient wood is challenging because suitable comparative material is scarce. The timbers are also expected to undergo magnetic resonance imaging in Halle to reveal additional information about their internal structure. Further dives will attempt to establish the extent of the archaeological remains and determine whether the individual pieces of worked wood were connected.

For now, the evidence supports the presence of Mesolithic people at the ancient lakeshore, but not yet the existence of a permanent settlement. Determining whether the timbers belonged to a hut, another type of structure or separate activities will be one of the central questions of future research at Lake Arendsee.
doesnt_show: The finds do not yet show whether the timbers formed part of a dwelling or how long the site was used.
settle: Targeted dives that map the spatial relationship between the worked timbers and any associated features.
